An enormous palm frond, scarred and pitted, stands beside the stationery shop in Papeete. A billboard advertising bikinis looms over the bus terminal in a bustling Bohemian coal town. In the photography studio, a fleeting pause: what circumstances led me to be captured in this particular glow? A scholar's rose-colored notecard bears his remarks on a single verse from Homer's epic. A negligent mail carrier abandoned letters in a sack marked "Bound for: The Azores." Everything unfolded quite differently than we'd anticipated during our night classes. Nobody knows who will eventually deliver the address that rallies a legion of warriors. Combat robots dominated the box office back when our grandchildren's children still frequented cinemas. So what now? How am I meant to fill my hours, given that the world's fair concluded ages ago? Deep-sea explorers stumbled upon it far from any shoreline: a golden player piano resting on the ocean floor. Serenity pervades images saturated with dreamlike quality in this fictional realm masquerading as reality.

outputs.L3:
# Fragments of an Unrecognizable World

The passage moves like memory itself—associatively, without warning, stitching together images that share no obvious lineage except the fact that they occurred, somewhere, to someone. A palm leaf in Papeete, its surface scarred perhaps by wind or by a hand that once carved initials into it, sits alongside a billboard in some forgotten Bohemian mining town, where a woman in a bikini smiles down at men who have likely never seen an ocean. These images do not explain each other. They simply coexist, the way disparate moments in a life coexist in the mind long after their original context has dissolved. What emerges is not a narrative but a texture—a fragmented sense of place, as though the world itself has become a collage of postcards sent from lives we did not quite live, memories we cannot fully claim as our own.

Within this scattering of images, a small, almost domestic scene interrupts: a hesitation in a photo studio, the pause before the shutter clicks. This instant, seemingly trivial, opens onto something larger—the question of how identity is fixed, framed, and handed back to us as an image we must then recognize as ourselves. Who decides the angle of light that will define a face for years to come? The hesitation suggests an awareness that being photographed is a kind of surrender, an agreement to be seen in a manner we do not fully control. It is a small crisis of selfhood, disguised as a moment of technical adjustment.

This uncertainty about how one is perceived extends outward into questions of how knowledge itself is transmitted and lost. The philologist's careful annotations on the *Iliad*—scholarly, precise, devoted to recovering meaning from an ancient and fragmentary text—stand in quiet counterpoint to letters addressed to the Azores that never arrived, swallowed by distance or bureaucracy or simple human error. Both cases speak to the same melancholy truth: that meaning does not always reach its destination. Words are sent, encoded, translated, annotated, and still they may fail to land where they were meant to. The scholar's diligence and the letter's silence are two faces of the same failure—the failure of intention to survive the passage from one mind to another.

This sense of failed transmission bleeds into a broader disillusionment with the present moment itself. The future, it turns out, arrived nothing like it was promised. The evening courses once taken with such earnest hope—courses meant to prepare one for a coming world of progress, order, perhaps even utopia—now seem almost comic in their naivety. Reality did not unfold according to the syllabus. Instead, it became something stranger, messier, and far less coherent than anything imagined in those classrooms, where the future was sketched out in confident diagrams that reality has since crossed out entirely.

It is fitting, then, that the passage closes on an image both absurd and strangely peaceful: a yellow pianola resting at the bottom of the sea, silent, its keys stilled by water rather than by any human hand. There is something deeply calming about this impossible tableau, precisely because it no longer strains to make sense. The world, the text suggests, has become a "banana republic of the real"—a place where the rules of plausibility have been suspended, where the surreal governs with the same casual authority that logic once claimed. And yet within this chaos there is an odd serenity, as though once one accepts that reality has abandoned its old order, one may finally rest within its stranger, more dreamlike arrangement—finding, at the bottom of an inexplicable sea, a kind of eerie, unearned peace.
outputs.L4:
The palm leaf keeps its scar the way a mouth keeps a secret—a thin white seam running lengthwise, as if something had once tried to write there and failed, or succeeded and been erased. You find it pressed between the pages of a book you don't remember buying, in a language you no longer speak fluently, if you ever did. The scar doesn't heal. It just becomes part of the leaf's design, the way old wounds become part of a face.

Down the road, or perhaps in another country entirely, a billboard rises forty feet into a sky the color of old photographs. A woman in a bikini smiles at a horizon she cannot see, her skin the exact shade of promises made in currencies that no longer exist. The billboard has been there so long that birds nest in the gap behind her painted knee. Children who grew up beneath her, learning their first words in her shadow, now bring their own children to point at the fading blue of her swimsuit, the cracking gloss of her teeth.

In the photo studio—was it Manila, was it Beirut, does it matter—a young woman stands with her hand not quite touching the small of her back, uncertain whether this is the pose she was told to strike or one she invented in the space between the photographer's instruction and her own body's memory of being looked at. The flash hasn't gone off yet. It may never go off. She holds her breath in a perpetual almost, waiting to become an image, already half-erased by the anticipation of her own disappearance into paper and chemical.

Meanwhile, in a room that smells of dust and tallow candles, an ancient philologist annotates a manuscript no one will read for another three hundred years. His marginalia branch like roots seeking water that isn't there: this word means loss, but also harvest; this phrase, mistranslated for centuries, actually describes the specific blue of a bruise three days old. He does not know that his notes will end up wrapped around fish in a market stall in a city that does not yet exist, in an empire whose name has not yet been spoken.

The letters, meanwhile, continue their errant journeys—addressed to streets renamed, to people relocated or deceased, to countries that dissolved and reformed under different flags. Somewhere, a letter meant for a lover in Odessa arrives instead in Valparaíso, is opened by a stranger who reads it as poetry, who does not understand a word but weeps anyway at the shape of longing on the page, at the particular slant of handwriting that suggests urgency, or grief, or both.

And beneath the water—which water, it hardly matters, all waters have become the same water now—a pianola sits in perfect silence, its perforated rolls swollen and disintegrating, the mechanism that once turned paper into music now turning only into rust and sediment. Fish swim through where hands once would have rested. The songs it played are gone, but something of their rhythm persists in the way current moves through its broken keys, a ghost tempo, a drowned waltz.

None of these things belong together. That is precisely the point. We have entered an era where the palm leaf and the billboard, the photograph and the philologist's ink, the misdirected letter and the submerged instrument, exist in the same instant, accessible, equal, and equally meaningless in their profusion. This is what reality has become: a banana republic of images, a small tropical nation of the mind where anyone can seize power for a moment, where currencies inflate and collapse within the span of a single scrolling gesture, where history no longer accumulates but simply piles up, image upon image, without hierarchy, without the old scaffolding of before and after, cause and consequence.

We used to believe in a shared story—that the philologist's careful marginalia would connect, somehow, to the woman on the billboard, that the letter would find its intended reader, that the pianola's music would drift up through the water and reach shore, transformed but recognizable. Now we understand there is no such connection, only the appearance of connection, the aesthetic pleasure of juxtaposition mistaken for meaning. The scarred palm leaf does not remember what cut it. The photo studio moment does not resolve into a photograph. We stand at the threshold of so many almost-images, so many nearly-stories, and call this abundance, when it might be better named by its older word: exile.
outputs.L5:
# Papeete: The Bohemia of the Pacific

The city of Papeete, capital of French Polynesia, has long attracted artists, writers, and wanderers seeking their own version of Bohemia beneath the palm trees. Nestled on the island of Tahiti, Papeete emerged in the nineteenth century as a small colonial outpost, yet it quickly became legendary far beyond its modest size, largely due to the creative souls who passed through its harbor.

The most famous of these wandering spirits was Paul Gauguin, who arrived in the late 1800s seeking an escape from European conventions and the constraints of bourgeois society. Papeete, for him and others like him, represented a kind of tropical Bohemia—a place where the rigid rules of Paris or London seemed to dissolve in the humid air, replaced by a freer, more sensory way of life. Gauguin's paintings, filled with vivid colors and mythic imagery of Tahitian life, cemented Papeete's reputation as a haven for those disillusioned with Western modernity.

Writers, too, found inspiration in this unusual meeting point of cultures. Robert Louis Stevenson, Somerset Maugham, and later James Michener all wrote about the town's peculiar charm—the mix of French colonial architecture, Polynesian tradition, and transient sailors and dreamers who passed through its streets and cafés. The waterfront bars of old Papeete became meeting places for an eclectic crowd: pearl traders, escaped convicts, remittance men, and artists all rubbing shoulders in a setting that felt worlds away from European respectability.

Today, Papeete has modernized considerably, with much of its Bohemian past existing more in memory and literature than in physical reality. Cruise ships now dock where schooners once anchored, and the market stalls sell souvenirs to tourists rather than provisions to sailors. Yet the town retains an undeniable allure, a residue of its wild reputation.

The idea of Papeete as a Bohemia—a place of reinvention and escape—speaks to a broader human desire: the wish to leave behind the constraints of one's origins and discover, in some distant harbor, a different version of oneself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in short fragmentary images, as if translated from German, ending with the tag "Translated from the German."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weather of Rooms

The clock in the hallway keeps the time of a country that no longer exists.

Someone has folded the afternoon into a small paper boat and set it on the windowsill, where it waits for a flood that will not come, or has already come, and this is what remains after.

The mother is made of tallow. She melts a little more each Sunday. No one mentions it. We simply move the chairs back from wherever she has been sitting.

A door in the ceiling. Nobody climbs to it. But the ladder is always freshly dusted.

*

In the garden: teeth growing where the tulips should be. The gardener wears his father's hands, borrowed, too large, the fingers dragging in the soil like rakes.

*

I ate the name of the town where I was born. It tasted of tin and horses. Now when I speak, small gray birds fall out of my mouth and lie stunned on the tablecloth until someone's aunt revives them with a sugar cube.

*

The war is kept in a drawer with the spoons. Sometimes at night you can hear it turning over, trying to find a comfortable position, metal against metal, unable to sleep.

*

Grandfather's coat hangs in the closet still breathing. We have stopped opening that door.

*

There is a lake beneath the house. We have always known this. When it rains, the furniture grows heavy with memory and sinks a little further into the floorboards, as if trying to reach the water, as if the water were an answer.

*

Someone is always leaving through a window that isn't there. We wave anyway. It seems the correct thing to do.

Translated from the German.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem made of disconnected, dreamlike vignettes—exotic locales, old letters, sunken objects—that reads like a translation from another language.
counterfactuals.output:
# Atlas of Drowned Correspondences

*

The postman drowned in 1911 and still
the letters arrive, salt-stiff,
addressed to no one in a handwriting
that dissolves when read twice.

*

In Valparaíso the women hang their husbands'
shirts like flags of countries
that no longer exist. The wind
reads them like braille.

*

I found your name
carved into the belly of a fish
in a market in Kochi. The fishmonger said,
*this one has been swimming for years,
looking for the sentence that owns it.*

*

Grandmother kept a jar of Black Sea water
on the windowsill. When the light hit it
at four o'clock, small ships appeared,
sailing toward the label,
which read: *fragile, this way up.*

*

The clocks in Trieste run backward
on Sundays. No one remembers why,
only that a bell disappeared into the Adriatic
and the town has been listening for its echo
ever since, tuning its silence.

*

Somewhere a chandelier still burns
at the bottom of a lake, in a ballroom
no one built. The fish that live there
have learned to waltz badly,
bumping into the corners of drowned mirrors.

*

*Dear R,* the letter begins,
*the peaches this year taste like the war
we didn't have. I send you
a photograph of the border,
which is only a photograph of grass.*

*

In Zanzibar, a woman sells hourglasses
filled with sand from beaches
that have since become other beaches.
*Time is a rumor*, she tells the tourists,
*that keeps changing its clothes.*

*

I keep your telegram in a tin
with the burnt sugar and the dried fig.
STOP. It says. STOP.
As if stopping were a place
one could arrive at, and stay.

*

The lighthouse keeper's daughter
married the fog. Their children
are the small gray birds
that land on ships at dawn
speaking languages no sailor understands.

*

At the bottom of the sea
there is a piano still playing
the last song anyone danced to
before the water came up
politely, like a guest who stayed too long.

*

This is not a translation.
This is what the original
would have said, if it had survived
the crossing, if the ship
had not been named
*Forgetting*, if the sea
were not also a kind of grammar
we keep almost learning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece in the style of a European avant-garde poet, using juxtaposed images (a scarred palm leaf, a bikini billboard, a philologist's index card) and ending with a note indicating translation from German.
counterfactuals.output:
**Card Catalogue for a Burned Season**

*i.*
A palm leaf, scarred—
someone's initials cut
into green, healing brown,
the wound outliving
the hand that made it.

*ii.*
Across the road, forty feet
of woman in a strip of flag-colored cloth,
selling the horizon back to itself.
No scar on her. No leaf.
Only voltage, only noon,
only the smile that is rented by the hour.

*iii.*
In a drawer that smells of Marburg, of dust,
a card holds one word, typed twice for certainty:
*Wunde.* Wound.
Beneath it, in pencil: *cf. Narbe, cf. Sonne,
cf. Ferien*—cross-referenced,
alphabetized, forgiven of all bleeding.

*iv.*
The leaf keeps drying in no particular hurry.
The woman keeps smiling from her scaffolding of light.
The card sleeps in its box like a small closed eye,
learning nothing, forgetting nothing,
filing the century under *W* for *what happened here.*

*v.*
Between them I could not say
which was the specimen,
which was the price,
which was already a fossil
being kept, so patiently, in order.

—translated from the German of Greta Anholt
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a list-form poem blending nostalgia, futurism, and mundane oddities (postmen, pianolas, world expositions), with a fragmented, translated feel.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory of Vanished Tuesdays

I.

The postman came on Tuesdays,
carrying letters from cities that no longer
answer to their names.

He wore his cap like a small
apology.

II.

At the Exposition of 1889,
they promised us the future
in a glass dome—
copper birds that sang
without ever having been alive.

We believed them.
We still believe them,
a little,
on Sundays.

III.

The pianola in my grandmother's parlor
played itself
for company.

Nobody wrote those songs.
They simply arrived,
punched into paper
like a language
made entirely of absence.

IV.

*Note: translation uncertain here—
the original word means both
"telegraph" and "the ache of waiting."*

V.

Catalogue of things promised by 1975:
— a car that folds into a suitcase
— dinners in pills, gray and efficient
— no more Tuesdays, only a single
    gleaming Now

None of this arrived.
The postman still comes.
The pill dinners rot
in a museum case
between the copper bird
and a photograph
of someone's optimism.

VI.

My mother kept a program
from the World's Fair,
folded so many times
the future had crease-marks,
had to be handled
like a wound.

VII.

Somewhere a pianola
is still playing
a song no one requested,
in a house that may or may not
still be standing—

*translator's note: the tense
here is deliberately broken,
as if the house exists
in two centuries
arguing with each other.*

VIII.

The postman retires.
No one replaces him.
The letters simply
stop,

the way a modern thing
stops—
not with a bang,
but with a small
grayed-out icon,

meaning: *delivered,*
meaning: *nothing
is coming.*

IX.

And still, some Tuesday,
I expect the knock.
I expect the copper bird
to open its beak
at last
and say something
true.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# The Clockmaker's Daughter

*after no one, in the manner of translation*

The hours hang in the cellar like smoked meat.
My grandmother's tongue, still speaking,
grows moss in the space between the walls.

I have seen the river forget its own name
three times before breakfast—
each time the fish grew a little more honest,
a little more like stones.

There was a winter that lived in our clock.
It wound itself backward through the brass teeth,
patient as a widow counting bread.
We did not notice until the frost
began speaking in our father's voice,
asking for the salt, asking
what year it was, asking
if the dead still required supper.

Memory is a barn that burns
without the courtesy of smoke.
You stand in the field and watch
the orange nothing eat the shape
of what you called *home*—
and still the cows come walking through it,
unbothered, chewing.

I keep my mother's silence in a drawer
with the other silverware.
Some nights I take it out and hold it
to the window, where the moon
does its slow arithmetic on the glass,
subtracting us, subtracting us,
until only the frame remains—
that patient rectangle
where a face used to happen.

The clock in the hallway has stopped
believing in its own hands.
It tells no time now, only weather:
a small brass front moving in,
a low pressure system of dust
settling on the numbers
like snow that has given up
on ever being water again.
